children: By Suzanne Kapner | Photography by Lanna Apisukh for WSJ

Walk into a retailer these days and it is often hard to find help. Not at Aritzia. The minute you glance at a blazer, blouse or sweatshirt, a saleswoman is at your elbow, asking if she can find your size or suggest a pair of pants to match.

These saleswomen don't just restock shelves or work the cash register. They help shoppers put outfits together. And they aren't shy about sharing their opinions, whether something looks great or misses the mark. Aritzia calls them style advisers.  "We chose that name intentionally," said Aritzia Chief Executive Jennifer Wong in an interview earlier this year. She joined the company in 1987 as a part-time style adviser. "They're not a sales associate. They're styling you."

It is the type of bespoke service often found at higher-end retailers-and part of the $2.7 billion clothing chain's allure. Aritzia has built a following among young women based on what it calls "Everyday Luxury." The idea is that you shouldn't have to be wealthy to afford high-quality clothes sold at beautiful boutiques with personalized service.

The strategy has fueled its explosive growth. Annual revenue has more than quadrupled over the past five years. Its shares are up nearly 700% since its initial public offering in 2016. And it is planning to add more than 100 new U.S. stores to the 77 it had as of July. In February, it announced the acquisition of Fred Segal, the iconic Los Angeles retailer known for showcasing emerging labels.

"The first time I walked into an Aritzia store, I was like, 'This is amazing,'" said Gabriella Ferguson, who is 18 years old and a freshman at Iowa State University. "It has a luxurious feel. But it's affordable enough for me."

Style advisers are key to the brand's aspirational positioning. Their high-touch approach is a departure from most mass-market chains, which have been cutting store staff in recent years as they funnel money into e-commerce, though some have started to reverse course.

At true luxury retailers, personal stylists are rainmakers who generate hefty sales for their employers. When Nordstrom poached personal stylist Catherine Bloom from Neiman Marcus last year, it was big news in fashion circles.
Aritzia's style advisers are expected to hit aggressive sales goals or risk being fired, according to former employees with knowledge of its hiring practices.

The advisers are also expected to look a certain way. Former Aritzia employees who worked as recruiters, managers and senior executives say hiring is largely based on physical appearance-with thin, pretty women getting preference over less attractive candidates. Aritzia denies the assertion.

Federal law prohibits employers from discriminating based on characteristics such as race, color, religion, sex and national origin as well as age and disabilities. There are also federal, state and local laws that prohibit discrimination based upon pregnancy. In some jurisdictions such as Michigan, New York City and San Francisco, it is against the law to discriminate based on height and weight.

It is legal to hire based on looks as long as it isn't tied to one of those protected characteristics, and physical attractiveness has always featured prominently in fashion. Employees are generally expected to project the image of their brand. But some of the former Aritzia employees, who have also worked for other retailers, including middle-market and luxury chains, said Aritzia's fixation on looks goes beyond the industry norm.

Recruiters responsible for hiring style advisers judge candidates on several criteria, including motivation, values and personality. But by far the most important criterion is style, which former employees say is largely a euphemism for physical attractiveness.

Candidates are scored on a scale of one to 10 on the four main factors, and need a combined score of at least 32 to get hired. But even if they score tens in the other categories, a style score below 8 could rule them out.
Being overweight or having acne are disqualifying factors, said the former employees, who described what they considered an institutional practice, even though it wasn't codified in company policies.

An Aritzia spokeswoman said the company's hiring decisions are based on several criteria of which style is one factor. But style, she said, isn't a proxy for physical attractiveness. Instead, it is meant to gauge candidates' interest in fashion and their understanding of the Aritzia brand. She added that no single criterion is weighted above the others and that Aritzia's employees reflect a range of backgrounds, ages, ethnicities and body types. She also denied that physical characteristics such as weight or skin condition could disqualify applicants.

She said that style advisers are assessed on more than just sales goals. They are also judged on teamwork, accountability, integrity and how they interact with clients. About one quarter of Aritzia's more than 6,000 boutique employees are style advisers. It employs roughly 8,800 people in total.

The chain got its start in Vancouver, British Columbia, when Brian Hill, a Canadian retail scion, opened the first boutique in 1984 in a shopping center there. He made up the name, choosing one that started with "A" to get a top spot in the mall's directory.

To differentiate itself from other mall-based competitors, Aritzia adopted the phrase "Everyday Luxury." Its stores are decorated with cream and beige color schemes, tiled floors, archways, wood fixtures and soft lighting, making them feel like expensive boutiques. Natural fibers like cotton, cashmere and silk feature prominently in its clothes, a departure from other midmarket retailers that have turned to cheaper synthetics. The classic cuts project a quiet luxury vibe along the lines of Loro Piana or Zegna.
But the pricing is anything but snobby, which has helped make its $148 Effortless Pants an office staple and its Super Puff down jacket, starting at around $250, go viral.
Having sales associates offer personal styling services completes the illusion of shopping in a far more upscale store. The advisers also act as walking billboards for the brand.

Natalie Nguyen, a former Aritzia style adviser, said young girls would come into the store where she worked in Tysons, Va., and ask her what she was wearing and how they could get the look. "They all want to be an Aritzia girl," she said.
Hill stepped down as CEO in 2022 but remains executive chair and continues an active role in the company.

Some former employees involved in recruitment said that Hill has at times taken photos of employees whose looks he didn't like during store visits. Some of those former employees said the staffers were then eased out or terminated.

The Aritzia spokeswoman said Hill doesn't take photos of specific employees. He also doesn't direct recruitment procedures and hasn't been directly involved in store-level hiring or firing decisions for more than two decades, according to the spokeswoman. "Aritzia has never terminated an employee because of his or her physical characteristics," she said.

One way that Aritzia creates encounters between style advisers and its shoppers is in the dressing rooms: They generally don't have mirrors. Instead, shoppers exit curtained-off cubicles to share floor-to-ceiling communal mirrors. "Boyfriend couches" are strategically placed nearby, where significant others can relax while their partners try on clothes. The setup is designed to foster a community atmosphere, as if you are trying on clothes at home with your besties. It is also an ideal opportunity for style advisers to pitch add-ons to your outfit.  Ferguson said she loves the arrangement. "All us girls are there hyping each other up," she said.  But it has created some negative pushback in social-media posts where shoppers complain about the aggressive sales environment. "It's like a runway and you are being judged by these perfect style advisers and someone's boyfriend," said Sudana Krasniqi, who wrote a substack post last year called "Hell is Aritzia Fitting Room."

The Aritzia spokeswoman said the shared mirrors are designed to help clients view their looks and foster a sense of community, while allowing them to get personalized styling guidance. For those who want more privacy, mirrored rooms are available upon request.
Wong, in the interview earlier this year, said that the communal mirrors aren't for everyone. "But for the most part," she said, they are "an aspect of our store experience that is very positive."
